hub.description: Planning a deck or fence in Gallatin, TN? What changes on an Old Hickory Lake lot, in a golf course HOA, or on a new subdivision yard.
hub.intro: Where your house sits in Gallatin shapes a deck or fence project more than most people expect. On Old Hickory Lake, the first question is where your lot ends and Corps of Engineers land begins. Golf course neighborhoods have review boards with firm ideas about style. A yard in a new subdivision may be graded fill with a drainage swale along the back, and if you have an older house near the downtown square, you may need a word with the city before work starts. For the details, see our pages on [building a deck in Gallatin](/deck-builder-gallatin-tn/) and [fence installation in Gallatin](/fence-company-gallatin-tn/).

sections.heading: Lake lots along Old Hickory
paragraphs: Old Hickory Lake is a reservoir on the Cumberland River, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers manages it. That matters if your Gallatin home backs up to the water. On many lake lots, the strip nearest the shore belongs to the Corps and not to the homeowner. Before anyone sketches a deck reaching toward the view or a fence running down to the bank, you need to know where your line falls. A survey or recorded plat usually shows it. Anything past that line answers to Corps shoreline rules, which sit apart from city permits.

Lake yards also tend to drop toward the water. A deck that starts level with the kitchen floor can end up tall at its outer edge, which calls for heavier posts and bracing, plus a railing on every open side. Fences on the same slope have to step down the hill or follow the grade. Plenty of lake lots near Gallatin, including some around Cages Bend, fall off this way, so it pays to walk the whole yard before talking about materials.

sections.heading: HOA review on golf course and lake lots
paragraphs: Golf course communities in Gallatin, including Foxland Harbor and Fairvue Plantation, have covenants, and in neighborhoods like these a deck or fence usually needs architectural review before it goes in. Rules differ from one neighborhood to the next, and sometimes between sections of the same one. In golf and lake neighborhoods, lots that back up to a fairway or the water can face limits on solid fencing, since boards often want to keep views open. Ask for the covenants and the submission form before you pick a style. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) explains what a clean packet includes.

sections.heading: New subdivisions on the edges of Gallatin
paragraphs: Gallatin keeps adding neighborhoods as it spreads out from town, and a new house usually comes with a bare yard and no fence. Builders often grade those lots with fill and cut a shallow swale along the back or side line to move storm water. A fence set tight across that swale can hold water in the yard next door. Easements for utilities and drainage often run right where people want a gate, so check your plat for them before the layout is final.

Decks on new homes bring their own quirks. Many builder houses in Gallatin have a back door with only a small landing or a short set of steps under it. A proper deck needs footings that reach firm soil below any loose fill, and it has to tie into the house framing correctly. If your neighborhood has an HOA, expect it to want plans for either project. In a subdivision that is still being built out, the builder or developer may still run that review, so ask who approves changes before you submit.

sections.heading: Older homes near downtown Gallatin
paragraphs: Downtown Gallatin has blocks of older houses around the square, and parts of the older town may fall under historic review. If your street might be one of them, ask the City of Gallatin planning office before you settle on a design. Where historic review applies, what faces the street usually gets the most attention, so a front yard fence tends to draw more questions than a deck behind the house. Older Gallatin lots bring other work too. Big shade trees put roots right where a post wants to go, and an old fence or deck often has to be torn out before anything new goes in.

sections.heading: Permits in the city and in Sumner County
paragraphs: A Gallatin mailing address does not always mean the house is inside Gallatin city limits. Some homes sit in unincorporated Sumner County, and that decides which office handles your permit. Attached or raised decks usually need one either way. Fences may need a permit or a zoning check depending on where you live. Rules change from place to place, so confirm with the city or county codes office and with your HOA before you commit. When you [request an estimate](#estimate), include your address and any HOA name so we can plan around both.

faqs.q: Can I build a deck from my Gallatin yard all the way down to Old Hickory Lake?
faqs.a: Often not. On many lots the ground closest to the shore belongs to the Corps of Engineers, and private decks generally are not allowed on it. Docks and paths to the water usually go through a separate Corps permit. Your deck has to stay on your own property, behind that line. Pull your survey first. If it is unclear where your ground ends, the Corps office that manages Old Hickory Lake can tell you what applies to your lot.

faqs.q: Does my Gallatin HOA have to approve a new fence or deck?
faqs.a: If your neighborhood has covenants, plan on it. Many HOAs in Gallatin's newer subdivisions and golf communities ask for a drawing and the location on your plat, along with the material and color. Approval is separate from any city or county permit, so you may need both. Start early, because review committees often meet on a set schedule. Building before approval can mean tearing work out later, which nobody wants to pay for twice.

faqs.q: On a new Gallatin lot, should the deck or the fence go in first?
faqs.a: In most Gallatin yards it makes sense to build the deck first, or at least plan both together. Deck work needs room to bring in lumber and sometimes a small machine, and a finished fence can block that path. Planning both at once also lets you line up the gate with the deck stairs. If the fence cannot wait because of a dog, a wide gate or a removable panel keeps the way open for later.

deck.description: Deck builder in Gallatin, TN: footings in clay and limestone, sloped Old Hickory Lake lots, golf course HOA review, and city or county permits.
deck.intro: Most Gallatin deck projects start at the back door with one question: how far out can this go, and how high will it sit? The lot answers most of it. Lake houses on Old Hickory often fall away toward the water, so a deck that starts at the kitchen floor can end well above the grass. Newer subdivision yards are usually flatter, but the top layer may be fill from grading. Any good deck builder should start with the ground and the rules for your address, and only then get to boards and railings.

sections.heading: Decks on sloped lake lots in Gallatin
paragraphs: On a lot that drops toward Old Hickory Lake, height is the main design decision. A taller deck needs heavier posts and bracing, plus a guardrail along every open edge. Stairs have to land somewhere sensible, which on a steep yard can mean a landing partway down. Some owners like the extra height because it frames the lake from inside the house. Others would rather step the deck down in two levels so it sits closer to the yard. Either choice can work, and the slope usually settles it.

The space under a tall lake deck deserves a plan too. Rain coming off the roof and down the hill will pass right through it, so gutter outlets need to be sorted out before footings are set. If you want to store kayaks or a mower under there, that changes post spacing. A Gallatin lake deck that faces west takes hard afternoon sun, which matters when you pick boards and a color.

sections.heading: Knowing where your lake lot ends
paragraphs: Before a deck plan grows toward the water, find your property line. Around Gallatin, much of the Old Hickory shoreline is Corps of Engineers land, and a private deck generally cannot sit on it. The boundary may be well back from where the grass meets the lake. Your survey or plat should show it, and if it does not, a surveyor can mark the corners. A deck built across that line can cause trouble when you sell, and the Corps can require an owner to remove a structure built on its land.

sections.heading: Footings in Gallatin clay and limestone
paragraphs: Many Gallatin yards have clay soil with limestone underneath, and in places the rock sits close to the surface. A footing hole may hit a ledge before it reaches the depth your codes office requires. When that happens, the fix depends on the rock and on what the inspector will accept, so it is better to learn about it before a big deck is priced than halfway through the build. Probing a few of the planned footing spots is the simple way to find out.

The clay itself is the other concern. It swells when wet and shrinks in a dry spell, and footings need to sit deep enough that this movement does not lift or drop the deck. Water drains through clay slowly, so a footing in a low corner of the yard can stay wet long after a storm. On new construction lots in Gallatin, the top layer is often fill spread during grading, and it may not be as firm as it looks. Footings belong in firm, undisturbed soil.

sections.heading: Deck rules in Gallatin golf course neighborhoods
paragraphs: In Foxland Harbor or Fairvue Plantation, as in other Gallatin neighborhoods with covenants, the review board sees your deck before the inspector does. Boards often look at railing style and board color. They may also ask whether the space under a raised deck will be skirted or left open. A deck that can be seen from a fairway or the lake may get a closer look. Ask for the written standards early, since some neighborhoods keep a list of approved colors or railing types. Designing to that list from the start saves you from redrawing plans after a rejection.

sections.heading: Wood or composite in Tennessee sun and lake humidity
paragraphs: Pressure treated pine is the common starting point for Gallatin decks. It costs less up front and takes stain well, but it needs cleaning and sealing on a regular schedule, and it will crack and turn gray if ignored. Composite boards skip the staining, though they can get hot underfoot in full afternoon sun, especially in darker colors. Near the lake, shade and moisture can grow mildew on either one. If you are weighing the two, our guide to [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) lays out the tradeoffs.

sections.heading: Tying a deck into a newer house
paragraphs: Newer homes in Gallatin subdivisions often have a back door with just a small builder landing under it. Attaching a deck there means taking the siding off where the ledger board goes and bolting that board to the house framing. Flashing over the ledger keeps water out of the wall. Where the back wall is brick veneer, a ledger cannot hang on the brick, so the deck usually stands on its own posts instead. On older houses near downtown Gallatin, the framing behind the siding can hold surprises, so it should be checked before anyone counts on it to carry weight. Mention the age of the house when you [request a deck estimate](#estimate).

sections.heading: Deck permits in Gallatin and Sumner County
paragraphs: An attached deck, or one raised well off the ground, usually needs a building permit. Which office issues it depends on whether your address is inside Gallatin city limits or out in the county, and your mailing address alone will not tell you. Expect inspections along the way, often at the footing stage and again at the end. Rules change, so confirm the details with the codes office that covers your address. Our guide on [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains the process in general terms.

Replacing an old deck counts too. Older decks were sometimes built with the ledger nailed to the house or with posts buried straight in the dirt, and a rebuilt deck has to meet the code in force today. An unpermitted deck can also slow down a sale, because buyers and their inspectors tend to ask about it. If you have an HOA, its approval is a separate step from the permit.

faqs.q: How tall can a deck be on a Gallatin lake lot?
faqs.a: There is no single number. The real limits come from what your codes office and HOA will approve. A taller deck is still buildable, but it needs heavier posts and bracing on careful footings, and some HOAs limit how far a deck can stand out from the house. A deck builder should draw the elevation to scale so you can see the real height before anything is framed.

faqs.q: What happens if you hit rock while digging deck footings?
faqs.a: In some Gallatin yards, limestone shows up before the hole is as deep as planned. The first step is to stop and see what is down there. Sometimes a footing can move a short way to miss a ledge, if the framing plan allows it. Other times the hole is drilled into the rock or the footing design changes. Either way, the inspector has to agree before concrete goes in. Expect rock to add some time and cost to the job.

faqs.q: Will my Gallatin HOA allow composite decking?
faqs.a: Many do, but some limit the colors or ask that railings match a set style. The only reliable answer is in your covenants and the review board's written standards. Send the board a sample or product sheet with your application, along with a drawing that shows where the deck sits on the lot. If your neighborhood has no HOA, the choice is yours, and the codes office will focus on the structure.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace an old deck in Gallatin?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, when the new deck is attached to the house or raised off the ground. Swapping boards on a sound frame may not need one, but rebuilding the frame or the ledger usually does. The answer depends on whether you are in city limits or the county, so call the codes office that covers your address. Keep the permit and inspection records, since buyers often ask for them later.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before calling a deck builder?
faqs.a: A copy of your survey or plat helps most, especially on a lake lot or a new subdivision lot with easements. Add your HOA rules if you have them, and a few photos of the back of the house that show doors and windows. Then think about how you want to use the space. A grill and a dining table need a different shape than a couple of chairs facing the lake.

fence.description: Fence installation in Gallatin, TN: privacy fence styles for new subdivisions, Corps lines on lake lots, golf course HOA rules and rocky post holes.
fence.intro: Most fence projects in Gallatin come down to one of two goals: a safe place to let the dog out, or some privacy from the house behind yours. Neither sounds complicated. The work gets harder on a lot that drops toward Old Hickory Lake, or where limestone sits a short way under the grass. HOA rules add another layer in many neighborhoods. This page covers what fence installation looks like on Gallatin lots, from the newest subdivisions out to the older streets near the square.

sections.heading: Privacy fences in new Gallatin subdivisions
paragraphs: New neighborhoods around Gallatin tend to put houses close together, with backyards that face each other across a shared line. A privacy fence is often one of the first projects owners take on after moving in. Board on board closes the gaps between pickets. Shadowbox, with pickets alternating on each side of the rails, blocks most of the view straight on and looks nearly the same from both yards. Plain side by side pickets leave small gaps as the wood dries. Our guide to [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) compares the common styles.

HOAs in newer Gallatin subdivisions often spell out the style and stain color. Some require the finished side to face the neighbor or the street, and many limit how far forward a fence can come along the side of the house. Get those rules in writing before you choose a design. A board can ask for changes after the fence is up, and moving a finished fence line costs far more than drawing it right the first time.

sections.heading: Property lines and drainage on newer lots
paragraphs: Before any post goes in, the line has to be clear. On newer Gallatin lots the corners are usually marked with pins, but pins get buried or knocked loose during landscaping. A survey settles it. Your plat will also show drainage and utility easements, and builders often grade a shallow swale along back lot lines to carry storm water. A solid fence dropped across that swale can back water into your yard or your neighbor's. Leaving a gap at the bottom, or running the fence beside the swale, usually solves it.

Tennessee 811 marks public utility lines at no charge before you dig, and making that call is required. It does not mark private lines, though. Sprinkler pipes, buried dog fence wire and power run out to a shed or yard light are the ones homeowners have to point out. Tell your installer about anything you know is down there, and read our guide on [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) before you talk with the neighbors.

sections.heading: Fencing a lake lot in Gallatin
paragraphs: On a lake lot, the boundary may not be where you think. Along much of Old Hickory Lake near Gallatin, the shoreline strip belongs to the Corps of Engineers, and private fences are generally not allowed there. Your fence has to stop at your line, which may sit well back from the water. Many lake owners also want to keep the view, so they fence only the sides of the yard, or pick an open style that a dog cannot squeeze through but people can see past.

Many lake yards also slope. A yard that falls toward the water needs panels that either step down in level sections or rack to follow the grade. Stepped panels look tidy but leave triangle gaps at the bottom, which matters with a small dog. Racked panels follow the ground more closely, though not every style can be racked. Our guide to [fencing a sloped yard](/guides/fence-on-a-slope/) walks through both. Damp ground near the lake is also hard on wood posts, so drainage around each post deserves attention.

sections.heading: Golf course lots in Gallatin HOA neighborhoods
paragraphs: If you live in a Gallatin golf community like Foxland Harbor or Fairvue Plantation, read the covenants before you pick a style. In golf course neighborhoods generally, lots that border the course or the lake can come with tighter fence rules than interior lots. Some boards allow only open styles on those edges, or no fence at all along the fairway side. Expect to submit a drawing that shows where the fence runs, along with the height and material. Having the approval letter in hand before the first hole is dug protects you if a neighbor complains later.

sections.heading: Setting fence posts in rock and clay
paragraphs: Rock is a common surprise in fence installation around Gallatin. Limestone sits close to the surface in some yards, and one hole on a run may go down clean while the next hits a ledge. On a straight run, that post can often move a little, with the panel beside it cut to fit. At a gate or a corner the post has to stay put, so the hole gets drilled into the rock instead. Rocky holes take longer to dig, so rock can raise a fence price.

Clay causes trouble after the post is set. Clay holds water, and a post sitting in a wet clay hole can loosen or rot at the base over time. Gate posts carry the most strain, so they usually get deeper holes and more concrete than line posts. Crowning the concrete so rain runs away from the wood helps. So does keeping mulch and soil from piling up against the posts.

sections.heading: Older lots near the downtown square
paragraphs: Near downtown Gallatin, some older streets may fall under historic review, and where it applies, a front yard fence is the kind of change reviewers tend to look at. Check with the city before you pick a style for the street side. Behind the house there is usually more freedom, though zoning still applies. Mature trees are the other factor on these lots. Big roots often cross the line right where posts need to go, and a post set too close can damage a tree you want to keep.

An old fence usually has to come out first, and its concrete footings often stay in the ground after the boards are gone. Those old footings sometimes sit right where the new posts belong, so they either get broken out or the new layout shifts to miss them. When you [request a fence estimate](#estimate), mention whether an old fence is coming out and roughly how long the run is.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence in Gallatin?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live. Inside city limits, a fence may need a permit or a zoning check, especially near a street or on a corner lot. Out in Sumner County the rules can be different. HOA approval is a separate step either way. Call the codes office for your address and confirm before work starts, since the answer can change with the height and location you want.

faqs.q: How tall can a privacy fence be in Gallatin?
faqs.a: No single answer fits every lot. Height limits come from zoning and from your HOA, and they are often lower in front yards than behind the house. Some golf course and lake neighborhoods set their own limits that are stricter than the city's. Check your covenants and the codes office for your address, then pick a privacy fence height that satisfies both. A taller fence also catches more wind, so posts matter more as height goes up.

faqs.q: Which side of the fence should face my neighbor?
faqs.a: Many Gallatin HOAs require the finished side to face out, toward the neighbor or the street, and it is a common courtesy even without one. With a shadowbox style, the two sides look nearly the same, which avoids the question. If your yard sits lower than the house next door, talk it through with your neighbor before posts go in so nobody is surprised by what they end up looking at.

faqs.q: Will a fence keep my dog in on a sloped lake lot?
faqs.a: It can, if the bottom edge is handled. Stepped panels leave triangle gaps on a hill, and a small dog will find them. Racking the panels to follow the grade keeps the line closer to the ground, and a bottom board can close what is left. For a dog that digs, wire along the base helps. Tell your fence company about your dog before the layout is drawn, since its size and habits change the plan.

faqs.q: Should I choose cedar or pressure treated pine for a fence in Gallatin?
faqs.a: Both are common around Gallatin. Pressure treated pine usually costs less, and it holds up well when the posts are set right. Cedar tends to twist and warp less than pine and weathers to gray if left alone, but it costs more. In humid Middle Tennessee summers, either one lasts longer with a sealer or stain applied once the wood is dry enough to take it. Some people use pressure treated posts with cedar pickets to get a bit of both.
